title: Power BI Gateway Monitoring - why is it so bad?
description: Power BI Gateway Monitoring - why is it so bad?
extracted:
| Topic | Practical advice / observation | Specific tools, APIs, endpoints, or details mentioned | What works / what doesn’t |
|---|---|---|---|
| Document what you want to manage first | “once you have documented what you want to manage, you can use the API to run checks and alert you when problems occur.” | Power BI REST API | Works as a general approach |
| List datasets in a workspace | Get a list of all datasets in a workspace, then use the dataset IDs for further checks | `https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/power-bi/datasets/get-datasets-in-group` | Works |
| Check scheduled refreshes | For each dataset ID, check when a refresh is scheduled | `https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/power-bi/datasets/get-refresh-schedule-in-group` | Works |
| Audit refresh history | For each dataset ID, audit refresh history and look for failures | `https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/power-bi/datasets/get-refresh-history-in-group` | Works |
| Check datasource status for a gateway | Example for other gateway monitoring questions: check status of datasources linked to a gateway | `https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/power-bi/gateways/get-datasource-status` | Works |
| Check gateway status | Check gateway status; you need another API to pull out all gateway IDs first | `https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/power-bi/gateways/get-gateway` | Works |
| PowerShell learning | “once you wrap your head around it and have learned a bit of powershell, it is pretty straight forward” | PowerShell | Helps make the API approach straightforward |
| Gateway logs limitation | Gateway logs do not cover dataflow refreshes currently | Gateway logs | Does **not** cover dataflow refreshes |
| Dataflows API limitation | “API's for Dataflows are not as robust as Datasets.” | Dataflows APIs | Weaker / less robust than dataset APIs |
| Power BI Sentinel | Suggested as something to buy if API-based monitoring is insufficient | “power bi sentinel” | Proposed alternative to DIY API monitoring |
| Azure SQL resources + Sentinel review | One commenter planned a meeting to price Azure SQL resources and have the review board look at Sentinel | Azure SQL resources, Sentinel | Used as part of a monitoring solution discussion |
| Desired built-in monitoring/UI | Commenter said the features should be baked into the Power BI web UI and not only available via an antiquated command-line solution | Power BI web UI, command-line solution | Current experience described as lacking / antiquated |
| Gateway monitoring pibx template | There is a “gateway monitoring pibx template” that “will give some insight” | Gateway monitoring pibx template | Provides some insight |
| Pull API data into a database | “pulling data from the APIs and storing it in a DB is helpful” | Power BI APIs, DB | Helpful |
| Limitation of API-to-DB approach | Storing API data in a DB “doesn't tell you anything about the internal workings of the gateways.” | Internal workings of the gateways | Not sufficient for internal gateway behavior |
| FUAM | “FUAM is supposed to help a lot” | FUAM | Expected to help a lot |
| FUAM limitation | “it is so brand spanking new it is still wet behind the ears and requires Fabric.” | Fabric | Very new; requires Fabric |
| Microsoft monitoring template | Reference to Microsoft’s gateway performance monitoring article/template | `https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/data-integration/gateway/service-gateway-performance` | Used to get more detailed monitoring |
| Write out performance logs | Update gateway configs to write out performance logs as described in the article | Gateway configuration, performance logs | Enables further analysis |
| Folder connector approach | Use the folder connector because the logging destination local path will exist on each gateway | Folder connector | Suggested way to ingest logs into a dataset |
| Ingest logs into a dataset | Pull gateway performance logs into a dataset to answer monitoring questions | Dataset, gateway logs | Works for questions about refreshes and more |
| Limited default monitoring data | “I wasn’t overly stoked with the amount of monitoring data I could get back by default.” | Default monitoring data | Not enough by default |
| VM down / gateway service down | These monitoring tasks “usually fall under the scope of IT Operations” | VM down, gateway service down, IT Operations | Often handled outside Power BI monitoring |
| Collect your own monitoring via APIs | If you want to collect your own, Power BI APIs are an alternate | Power BI APIs | Alternative, but not necessarily ideal |
| API collectors usefulness caveat | Collectors hitting the APIs are “not overly useful information to have” compared with the effort unless you’re responsible for the gateway servers | API collectors | Arguably not worth the effort for some cases |
| Monthly report to detect abusive refresh rates | Run a report once a month that looks for refresh rates under 1 hour and stop them before they get out of hand | Report querying SQL database logs | Works to catch abusive scheduling behavior |
| SQL database logs approach | Created a report from scratch querying the SQL database logs to find problematic refresh rates | SQL database logs | Works, but was described as insane / hard to track down |
| Performance monitoring via query duration | The Microsoft monitoring template can show how many milliseconds a query took | Monitoring template, milliseconds per query | Available, but described as pretty irrelevant by the author |

| Explicitly stated monitoring problems / limitations | Details |
|---|---|
| Can’t tell how many scheduled refreshes occur at noon | Stated by the original poster |
| Multiple queries fail at 11 PM, unclear which datasets are affected | Stated by the original poster |
| Can’t count number of failed refreshes today | Stated by the original poster |
| Gateway going offline or datasource connection failing | Mentioned as issues the author wants to catch |
| Need to watch the manage gateways page around the clock? | Asked as a concern |
| Gateway logs don’t cover dataflow refreshes currently | Stated by `nelson_fretty` |
| Dataflows APIs are not as robust as Datasets | Stated by `nelson_fretty` |
| Default gateway monitoring data is limited | Stated by `Analytiks` |
| Internal workings of gateways are not revealed by API-to-DB logging alone | Stated by `RandomChance` |
| Many monitoring features are not baked into the Power BI web UI | Stated by `jcampbell474` |
| Power BI administration and tracking tools need improvement | Stated by `BranWafr` |

| Specific issue reported | Exact detail |
|---|---|
| Refresh abuse via very frequent schedules | Users set refresh rate to every 1 minute or every 5 minutes to simulate live connections |
| Impact of abusive refreshes | Reports were delayed by almost 28 hours |
| Cause of delay | A report running every 1 minute kept the queue growing because Power BI puts reports in the queue when busy |
| Detection method used later | A report once a month looking for refresh rates under 1 hour |
| Mitigation | Stop them before they get out of hand |
